title: Stem Cell Therapy (Awareness Level)
desc: Understand in plain words what stem cells are, what approved treatments exist, how to spot unproven clinics, and the ethics involved. Awareness only.
outcomes: Explain what stem cells are and the main types.
Use a checklist to judge a clinic or advert.
Separate approved uses from experimental claims.
Weigh hope against evidence and cost.
Draft a short guide for patients and families.
task: Produce a one-page safe-choice guide on stem cell treatments with a clinic checklist and a glossary.
condition: A computer, public information, two peers and a mentor. No medical advice is given and no patient records are used.
standard: Facts are sourced and dated; approved and experimental uses are kept apart; no promise of cure appears; the guide tells readers to ask a qualified specialist; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Patients, carers, teachers, health writers and trainee lab staff.
modules: What stem cells are
Understand
Stem cells can make copies of themselves and become other cell types.
Types: embryonic, adult (tissue) and induced stem cells.
Each type has different uses and limits.
Most bodies already use stem cells every day, for example in blood and skin.
Blood stem cells in bone marrow keep making new blood cells through life.
Draw a simple picture of one stem cell becoming two kinds.
Picture is accurate.
Approved uses
Understand
Some treatments are established.
Blood stem cell transplants for certain blood cancers and disorders are long established.
Skin and eye surface grafts exist for some conditions.
Approval means tested trials and regulators agreed.
A hospital uses a donor transplant for a specific leukaemia after matching tests.
List three approved uses with their source.
Sources are public regulators or hospitals.
Trials and evidence
Analyse
Research moves in stages.
Lab studies, then small human trials, then larger trials, then approval.
Case stories are not proof.
Look for peer review, trial registries and large samples.
A clinic cites patient stories only; the learner finds no registered trial.
Check one claim against a trial registry.
Finding is written with date.
Unproven clinics
Evaluate
Some clinics sell hope without proof.
Red flags: cures many diseases, pay up front, no trial, no follow-up, pressure to decide fast.
Risks: infection, tumours, wasted money, delay of real care.
Ask: Is this approved or in a registered trial?
A family declines an expensive injection after the clinic cannot name any trial.
Score two adverts with the red-flag list.
Each red flag is cited.
Ethics and sources
Evaluate
Questions of consent and respect.
Donors must give informed, free consent.
Debates exist about embryo use; different cultures and faiths hold different views.
Cord blood banking is a personal choice, with limited common uses.
A parents' guide explains cord blood choices without pressure.
Write a balanced paragraph on one ethical question.
Both views are stated fairly.
Talking with specialists
Apply
Come prepared.
Questions: purpose, approval status, risks, cost, alternatives, follow-up.
Take a family member and notes.
A second opinion is normal.
A patient brings a one-page question list to the haematologist.
Make a question list.
Eight clear questions.
Cost, travel and safety
Evaluate
Medical travel adds risks.
Check licence and insurance; plan follow-up care at home.
Count the full cost, not only the fee.
Keep records of every treatment.
A traveller adds flights, hotel and follow-up to the price and decides against it.
Cost a hypothetical trip.
Total includes all items with currency.
Write the guide
Create
Make it useful.
One page, plain words, large print.
Include the checklist and local regulator contacts.
Test with two readers.
Readers say they would ask "is it in a registered trial?" first.
Finish and test.
Readers can repeat three red flags.
quiz: Name two stem cell types.
Adult (tissue) and embryonic (or induced). (Covered in module 1: What stem cells are. To pass that module: Picture is accurate.)
Name one long-established use.
Blood stem cell transplant for some blood disorders. (Covered in module 2: Approved uses. To pass that module: Sources are public regulators or hospitals.)
Are patient stories proof?
No. (Covered in module 3: Trials and evidence. To pass that module: Finding is written with date.)
Name two red flags.
Cures many diseases; pay up front or fast pressure. (Covered in module 4: Unproven clinics. To pass that module: Each red flag is cited.)
What question tests a clinic?
Is it approved or in a registered trial? (Covered in module 5: Ethics and sources. To pass that module: Both views are stated fairly.)
Name one risk.
Infection, tumours, wasted money or delayed care. (Covered in module 6: Talking with specialists. To pass that module: Eight clear questions.)
Why consent?
Donors must freely agree with full information. (Covered in module 7: Cost, travel and safety. To pass that module: Total includes all items with currency.)
Is a second opinion normal?
Yes. (Covered in module 8: Write the guide. To pass that module: Readers can repeat three red flags.)
What cost parts does travel add?
Flights, stay and follow-up. (Covered in module 8: Write the guide. To pass that module: Readers can repeat three red flags.)
Who gives medical advice?
Qualified specialists, not this course. (Covered in module 8: Write the guide. To pass that module: Readers can repeat three red flags.)
rubric: Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
Checked, dated and explained to others

ladder: What stem cells are

L1: learner can say what a stem cell is. Focus module: What stem cells are (Understand, 2 h). Stem cells can make copies of themselves and become other cell types. Key points: Types: embryonic, adult (tissue) and induced stem cells. Each type has different uses and limits. Most bodies already use stem cells every day, for example in blood and skin.

Teach: open with the worked example. Blood stem cells in bone marrow keep making new blood cells through life. Then set the activity: Draw a simple picture of one stem cell becoming two kinds. Mark against the standard: Picture is accurate. Check at this level: Name two stem cell types. Model answer: Adult (tissue) and embryonic (or induced). Simple drawing.
Approved uses

L2: learner can name approved uses. Focus module: Approved uses (Understand, 2 h). Some treatments are established. Key points: Blood stem cell transplants for certain blood cancers and disorders are long established. Skin and eye surface grafts exist for some conditions. Approval means tested trials and regulators agreed.

Teach: open with the worked example. A hospital uses a donor transplant for a specific leukaemia after matching tests. Then set the activity: List three approved uses with their source. Mark against the standard: Sources are public regulators or hospitals. Check at this level: Name one long-established use. Model answer: Blood stem cell transplant for some blood disorders. Use hospital pages.
Trials and evidence

L3: learner can read evidence stages. Focus module: Trials and evidence (Analyse, 2 h). Research moves in stages. Key points: Lab studies, then small human trials, then larger trials, then approval. Case stories are not proof. Look for peer review, trial registries and large samples.

Teach: open with the worked example. A clinic cites patient stories only; the learner finds no registered trial. Then set the activity: Check one claim against a trial registry. Mark against the standard: Finding is written with date. Check at this level: Are patient stories proof? Model answer: No. Explain trial stages.
Unproven clinics

L4: learner can use red flags on adverts. Focus module: Unproven clinics (Evaluate, 2 h). Some clinics sell hope without proof. Key points: Red flags: cures many diseases, pay up front, no trial, no follow-up, pressure to decide fast. Risks: infection, tumours, wasted money, delay of real care. Ask: Is this approved or in a registered trial?

Teach: open with the worked example. A family declines an expensive injection after the clinic cannot name any trial. Then set the activity: Score two adverts with the red-flag list. Mark against the standard: Each red flag is cited. Check at this level: Name two red flags. Model answer: Cures many diseases; pay up front or fast pressure. Use real adverts.
Ethics and sources

L5: learner can discuss ethics fairly. Focus module: Ethics and sources (Evaluate, 2 h). Questions of consent and respect. Key points: Donors must give informed, free consent. Debates exist about embryo use; different cultures and faiths hold different views. Cord blood banking is a personal choice, with limited common uses.

Teach: open with the worked example. A parents' guide explains cord blood choices without pressure. Then set the activity: Write a balanced paragraph on one ethical question. Mark against the standard: Both views are stated fairly. Check at this level: What question tests a clinic? Model answer: Is it approved or in a registered trial? Facilitate with care.
Cost, travel and safety

L6: learner can lead a patient-information desk. Focus module: Cost, travel and safety (Evaluate, 2 h). Medical travel adds risks. Key points: Check licence and insurance; plan follow-up care at home. Count the full cost, not only the fee. Keep records of every treatment.

Teach: open with the worked example. A traveller adds flights, hotel and follow-up to the price and decides against it. Then set the activity: Cost a hypothetical trip. Mark against the standard: Total includes all items with currency. Check at this level: Name one risk. Model answer: Infection, tumours, wasted money or delayed care. Cover roles.
Write the guide

L7: learner can audit a guide. Focus module: Write the guide (Create, 2 h). Make it useful. Key points: One page, plain words, large print. Include the checklist and local regulator contacts. Test with two readers.

Teach: open with the worked example. Readers say they would ask "is it in a registered trial?" first. Then set the activity: Finish and test. Mark against the standard: Readers can repeat three red flags. Check at this level: Why consent? Model answer: Donors must freely agree with full information. Peer audit.
